title: Everyday Serbo-Croatian: handwritten lesson bank
description: Thirty individually authored lessons from first contact through lower-intermediate review. Levels are editorial guides, not a CEFR certification. Examples prioritize Serbian and Montenegrin while showing supported forms used across Serbian, Montenegrin, Croatian and Bosnian.
language_notes: The four standards share a large common base, and forms cross borders. Regional labels describe useful tendencies, not exclusive national ownership. Serbian and Montenegrin use both Latin and Cyrillic; Croatian is normally written in Latin, and Bosnian is commonly written in Latin and also Cyrillic. Every lesson awaits native-speaker review.
answer_policy: Each exercise lists accepted answers explicitly. A client may normalize Unicode to NFC, case, surrounding whitespace and terminal punctuation, but must preserve meaningful diacritics. An unlisted answer that may be valid should be shown beside the model answer for self-assessment instead of being declared wrong.
source_policy: Teaching explanations and original examples were written for this bank. A small number of authentic sentence examples are from the attributed Tatoeba pilot; their source and English-side contributor, sentence URL, export owner and CC BY 2.0 FR license are recorded on the example. Vocabulary selection was informed by data/sc_frequency_2000.json and research/sc_frequency_2000_sources.md. That candidate list is Croatian-web-corpus ranked and remains unreviewed.

lessons.title: Greet and introduce yourself
lessons.objective: Use a greeting, say your name and choose a polite or familiar question.
lessons.teaching_note: Dobar dan is a polite daytime greeting. Zovem se introduces a name. Kako ste? is polite singular or plural; Kako si? is familiar singular. The pronoun ja is often omitted when the verb already makes the person clear.

examples.english: Good day. My name is Ana.

examples.note: Tatoeba sentence labeled Bosnian; this greeting is broadly understood.

exercises.prompt: Which is a polite daytime greeting?
exercises.feedback: Dobar dan means good day. Laku noć means good night; hvala means thank you.

exercises.prompt: Write “My name is Ana.”
exercises.feedback: Zovem se Ana is the usual name-introduction formula.

exercises.prompt: Change the familiar question Kako si? to polite or plural address.
exercises.feedback: Replace si with ste to address someone politely or more than one person.

lessons.unit_objective: Greet people and introduce yourself.

lessons.title: Recognize both scripts
lessons.objective: Match familiar Latin spellings with Cyrillic and notice several distinct sounds.
lessons.teaching_note: Serbian and Montenegrin may be written in either script. A transliteration changes script, not the word. Latin č and ć are different letters; š and ž are also distinct. In Latin, lj, nj and dž are traditionally taught as alphabetic units and correspond to љ, њ and џ.

examples.note: Latin lj corresponds to one Cyrillic letter.

exercises.prompt: Which Latin phrase matches Добар дан?
exercises.feedback: Добар дан is Dobar dan, with the same words written in Cyrillic.

exercises.prompt: Write Zdravo in Cyrillic.
exercises.feedback: Здраво is the Cyrillic spelling of Zdravo.

exercises.prompt: Write the Cyrillic letter that corresponds to Latin nj.
exercises.feedback: Latin nj corresponds to the single Cyrillic letter њ.

lessons.title: Say who you are
lessons.objective: Use the present forms sam, si, je and smo in short introductions.
lessons.teaching_note: Biti means to be. Its short present forms include ja sam, ti si, on or ona je, mi smo, vi ste and oni or one su. The subject pronoun is optional in many ordinary sentences; include it when useful for emphasis or clarity.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Mi ___ ovde. (We are here.)
exercises.feedback: Smo is the present form of biti used with mi, “we.”

exercises.prompt: Translate: She is Ana.
exercises.feedback: Ona means she, and je is the present form of biti.

exercises.prompt: Remove the optional subject pronoun without changing the meaning: Ja sam Marko.
exercises.feedback: The subject ja is optional; place sam after the name: Marko sam.

lessons.title: Match adjective endings
lessons.objective: Use common masculine, feminine and neuter adjective forms.
lessons.teaching_note: Many adjectives change to agree with a noun's grammatical gender and number. Dobar, dobra and dobro are masculine, feminine and neuter forms of “good.” The noun's grammatical gender matters; it is not always the same as a person's gender.

exercises.prompt: Which greeting means “good morning”?
exercises.feedback: Dobro jutro means good morning. Dobar dan means good day; laku noć means good night.

exercises.prompt: Complete the phrase with the feminine form: ___ kuća (a big house).
exercises.feedback: Kuća is feminine, so use velika.

exercises.feedback: Gladan agrees with a masculine speaker; a woman commonly says Gladna sam.

lessons.title: Ask what something is
lessons.objective: Use šta or što, ovo and simple question forms.
lessons.teaching_note: Šta and što both mean “what”; preference varies by region and construction. Ovo means “this” or “this thing.” Intonation can form a yes-or-no question, and li is a common question particle. The authentic example below is labeled Bosnian in Tatoeba; the label does not claim exclusive usage.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase asks “What is this?”
exercises.feedback: Šta means what and ovo means this.

exercises.prompt: Translate: Who is this?
exercises.feedback: Ko asks who; je is “is,” and ovo is “this.”

exercises.prompt: Turn "Ovo je voda." into a yes-or-no question using Da li.
exercises.feedback: The pattern is Da li + verb + subject or complement: Da li je ovo voda?

lessons.title: Say yes, no and not
lessons.objective: Answer simple questions and place ne before an ordinary verb.
lessons.teaching_note: Da means yes and ne means no. For most ordinary finite verbs, ne comes before the verb: znam “I know,” ne znam “I do not know.” Some forms combine with the negative, such as nemam “I do not have”; learn those as whole forms.

exercises.prompt: What is the ordinary negative of znam, "I know"?
exercises.feedback: For this verb, put ne before znam.

exercises.feedback: Ne znam means “I do not know.”

exercises.prompt: You do not have water. Write “I don't have water.”
exercises.feedback: Nemam is the combined negative form of imam. Vodu is the object form of voda here.

lessons.title: Order a drink
lessons.objective: Make a polite request and recognize common feminine accusative forms.
lessons.teaching_note: A short request can end with molim, “please.” In Vodu, molim, voda changes to vodu because it is the thing requested. Similar everyday forms include kafu, kavu or kahvu, depending on the noun form a speaker uses.

examples.note: Kavu or kahvu are also used.

exercises.prompt: Which means “Water, please”?
exercises.feedback: Vodu is the object form in this short request; molim means please.

exercises.prompt: Order tea politely: “Tea, please.”
exercises.feedback: Čaj, molim is a natural short order.

exercises.prompt: Change voda to its object form in "Molim ___."
exercises.feedback: The feminine noun voda becomes vodu in this direct-object request.

lessons.title: Talk about family
lessons.objective: Name close family and make possessives agree with the noun.
lessons.teaching_note: Family vocabulary includes majka, otac, brat, sestra and porodica. Possessives such as moj, moja and moje change to agree with the thing owned: moj brat, moja sestra, moje dete. Dete is used in Ekavian speech; dijete is an Ijekavian form.

examples.note: Obitelj is also common, especially in Croatian.

exercises.prompt: Choose the usual phrase for “my sister.”
exercises.feedback: Sestra is feminine, so the possessive is moja.

exercises.prompt: Translate: This is my brother.
exercises.feedback: Moj agrees with the masculine noun brat.

exercises.prompt: Give a common Croatian alternative for porodica meaning “family.”
exercises.feedback: Obitelj is common in Croatian; porodica is widely understood too.

lessons.title: Count and ask the price
lessons.objective: Use small numbers and ask how much something costs.
lessons.teaching_note: Learn the numbers jedan, dva, tri, četiri, pet and deset in useful phrases. The form of one and two can agree with a noun's gender. Koliko košta? asks the price of one thing; kolika je cena/cijena? is another useful question for the price.

examples.note: The object form is used in this café order.

examples.english: How much does the tea cost?

examples.note: Dve is Ekavian; dvije is Ijekavian. Kafa/kava preferences also vary.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase asks the price?
exercises.feedback: Koliko košta? means “How much does it cost?”

exercises.prompt: Write “three” in the language.
exercises.feedback: Tri means three.

exercises.prompt: Ask how much tea costs.
exercises.feedback: Koliko košta + item asks how much that item costs.

lessons.unit_objective: Ask questions and handle simple purchases.

lessons.title: Make a simple plan
lessons.objective: Use today, tomorrow and a basic clock-time question.
lessons.teaching_note: Danas means today; juče or jučer means yesterday; sutra means tomorrow. Sjutra is also used in Montenegro. Koliko je sati? asks what time it is. Time expressions and date conventions can vary, so learn a practical phrase before memorizing a full counting system.

exercises.prompt: When is sutra?
exercises.feedback: Sutra means tomorrow; sjutra is another form used in Montenegro.

exercises.prompt: Ask: What time is it?
exercises.feedback: Koliko je sati? is the common time question.

exercises.prompt: Say “See you tomorrow,” using either common form.
exercises.feedback: Both sutra and sjutra are used; the choice depends on speaker and region.

lessons.unit_objective: Ask questions and handle simple purchases.

lessons.title: Ask where something is
lessons.objective: Ask for a place and use a simple location phrase.
lessons.teaching_note: Gde and gdje both mean where; gde is Ekavian and gdje is Ijekavian. Gde je hotel? asks where the hotel is. For a stationary location, u gradu means “in the city”; movement into the city is u grad.

examples.english: The hotel is in the city.
I am going to the city.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks where the hotel is?
exercises.feedback: Gde je hotel? and Gdje je hotel? both ask where the hotel is.

exercises.prompt: Translate: The hotel is in the city.
exercises.feedback: Use u gradu for a stationary location in the city.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the movement form: Idem ___ grad. (I am going to the city.)
exercises.feedback: With movement into the city, use u grad; for location, use u gradu.

lessons.title: Find the station
lessons.objective: Ask for the station and understand a few direction words.
lessons.teaching_note: Stanica is a broadly understood word for station; Croatian also commonly uses kolodvor for a railway station. Levo or lijevo means left, desno means right, and pravo means straight ahead. These words work with short direction phrases.

examples.note: Kolodvor is common in Croatian for a railway station.

exercises.prompt: What does desno mean?
exercises.feedback: Desno means right; pravo means straight and levo/lijevo means left.

exercises.prompt: Ask: Where is the station? Use either gde or gdje.
exercises.feedback: Both Gde je stanica? and Gdje je stanica? are useful forms.

prompt_segments.text: Ask: Where is the station? Use either

exercises.prompt: Tell a visitor to go straight ahead.
exercises.feedback: Idite is a polite or plural command; pravo means straight ahead.

lessons.title: Describe a daily routine
lessons.objective: Use a few present-tense verbs and time words in short statements.
lessons.teaching_note: Present-tense endings vary by verb. Learn each useful verb with its forms: raditi includes radim, radiš, radi; živeti/živjeti includes živim, živiš, živi. The ending often identifies the subject, so a pronoun can be omitted.

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ja ___ u gradu. (I live in the city.)
exercises.feedback: Živim is the first-person singular form.

exercises.prompt: Translate: I work today.
exercises.feedback: Radim is the first-person singular form of raditi.

exercises.prompt: Add the explicit subject "I" to Radim danas.
exercises.feedback: Ja can be added for emphasis or clarity, even though radim already marks first person.

lessons.title: Say what you can, want and need
lessons.objective: Use mogu, želim and trebam in practical requests.
lessons.teaching_note: Moći means to be able to; želim means I want or would like. Trebam and treba mi are both useful, though preferred constructions vary by region and sentence. Infinitive and da + present constructions are both used after some modal verbs; notice the form you hear locally.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means “I can help”?
exercises.feedback: Mogu means “I can”; da pomognem is one common construction.

exercises.prompt: Translate: I need help.
exercises.feedback: Treba mi pomoć is a common way to say “I need help.”

exercises.prompt: Politely say that you would like water.
exercises.feedback: Želim means I want or would like; vodu is the object form of voda.

lessons.unit_objective: Make plans and find your way.

lessons.title: Talk about tomorrow
lessons.objective: Make a simple future plan with ću and a verb.
lessons.teaching_note: A common future pattern uses a short form of hteti/htjeti with an infinitive: Sutra ću raditi, “Tomorrow I will work.” In ordinary writing, the short form can appear before or after the infinitive in a clause, as in ću doći and doći ću. Regional forms and placement deserve listening practice.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means “I will come tomorrow”?
exercises.feedback: Doći ću is a future form; sutra means tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Translate: I will work tomorrow.
exercises.feedback: Sutra ću raditi uses a future form of hteti plus the infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Ask a friend: “Will you come?”
exercises.feedback: Hoćeš li doći? is a familiar singular question.

lessons.unit_objective: Make plans and find your way.

lessons.title: Say what happened yesterday
lessons.objective: Build the past tense with an auxiliary and a gendered participle.
lessons.teaching_note: The usual past tense combines a short form of biti with an l-participle: Ana je došla, Marko je došao, and they su došli. The participle changes for gender and number. The auxiliary is often placed after the first stressed word.

exercises.prompt: Choose the usual form for a woman: Ana je ___.
exercises.feedback: Došla is the feminine singular participle.

prompt_segments.text: Choose the usual form for a woman:

exercises.prompt: Translate: Marko worked.
exercises.feedback: Je is the auxiliary, and radio is the masculine singular participle.

exercises.prompt: Join these into one sentence with a plural subject: Ana je došla. Marko je došao.
exercises.feedback: A masculine and feminine mixed group commonly takes došli with the plural auxiliary su.

prompt_segments.text: Join these into one sentence with a plural subject:
Ana je došla. Marko je došao.

lessons.title: Say what you see and want
lessons.objective: Use common accusative objects, including an animate masculine noun.
lessons.teaching_note: A direct object often changes form. Feminine voda becomes vodu; masculine animate čovek/čovjek becomes čoveka/čovjeka. Not every noun has the same visible ending, so learn frequent phrases with their cases.

exercises.prompt: Choose the usual object form: Vidim ___ (water).
exercises.feedback: Vodu is the direct-object form in this sentence.

exercises.prompt: Write “I see a man/person,” using either Ekavian or Ijekavian.
exercises.feedback: Čoveka is Ekavian; čovjeka is Ijekavian. Both are accepted.

exercises.prompt: Say that you see a woman.
exercises.feedback: Ženu is the object form of žena.

lessons.unit_objective: Describe actions, needs and places.

lessons.title: Talk about amounts and absence
lessons.objective: Recognize common genitive forms after quantities and nema.
lessons.teaching_note: The genitive appears in many patterns. Nema vode means “there is no water,” and čaša vode means “a glass of water.” Numbers above four often take a genitive plural, but number phrases have details and exceptions; learn common chunks first.

examples.english: I have a lot of time.

exercises.prompt: Complete the common phrase: Nema ___. (There is no water.)
exercises.feedback: Nema is commonly followed by the genitive; voda becomes vode.

exercises.prompt: Translate: A glass of water, please.
exercises.feedback: Vode is the genitive form after čaša in this phrase.

exercises.prompt: Say “I have a lot of time.”
exercises.feedback: Vremena is the genitive form used after mnogo in this expression.

lessons.title: Say who needs or receives something
lessons.objective: Use a basic dative recipient and the phrase treba mi.
lessons.teaching_note: The dative often marks a recipient or the person affected. In Treba mi voda, mi means “to me” and voda is the thing needed. For a named recipient, Ana gets the dative form Ani: Dajem Ani knjigu, “I give Ana a book.”

examples.english: I am giving Ana a book.

exercises.prompt: In Treba mi voda, what does mi mean?
exercises.feedback: Mi is the short dative pronoun meaning to me here.

exercises.prompt: Say: I need water.
exercises.feedback: Treba mi voda is a common impersonal pattern for “I need water.”

exercises.prompt: Change Ana to the recipient form: Dajem ___ knjigu.
exercises.feedback: Ani is the dative form of Ana.

lessons.unit_objective: Describe actions, needs and places.

lessons.title: Use common place prepositions
lessons.objective: Recognize movement, location and origin in short phrases.
lessons.teaching_note: U and na can take different cases depending on meaning: u gradu is location, u grad is movement into the city. Iz and od commonly take the genitive: iz grada means from the city; od prijatelja means from a friend. Learn the whole phrase with its meaning.

examples.english: I am waiting at the station.
I am going to the station.
I am coming from the city.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means “I am at the station”?
exercises.feedback: Na stanici expresses a stationary location; na stanicu expresses movement to it.

exercises.prompt: Translate: I am coming from the city.
exercises.feedback: Iz grada means from the city.

exercises.prompt: Choose the movement phrase for “I am going to the station.”
exercises.feedback: Na stanicu expresses movement toward the station; na stanici is a location.

lessons.unit_objective: Describe actions, needs and places.

lessons.title: Use everyday reflexive verbs
lessons.objective: Recognize se in common routines and reciprocal phrases.
lessons.teaching_note: Some verbs are commonly used with the reflexive clitic se, whose meaning depends on the verb. Zovem se is the name formula, perem se means I wash myself, and vidimo se means we will see each other. Do not translate se with one fixed English word in every phrase.

exercises.prompt: Which expression is the usual way to introduce your name?
exercises.feedback: Zovem se is the usual name-introduction formula.

exercises.prompt: Translate: See you later.
exercises.feedback: Vidimo se kasnije means “See you later.”

exercises.prompt: Explain briefly: Does se always translate as “self”?
accepted_answers: No; its meaning depends on the verb.
exercises.feedback: Se has different functions; in vidimo se it is reciprocal, while zovem se is a name formula.

lessons.title: Give a polite request
lessons.objective: Use polite or plural imperative forms in common requests.
lessons.teaching_note: The polite or plural imperative is useful with strangers: Recite, “Say/tell”; govorite, “speak”; čekajte, “wait.” Molim vas softens the request. Keep the verb and politeness marker together in useful chunks.

examples.english: Please say it one more time.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase politely asks someone to speak slowly?
exercises.feedback: Govorite is polite singular or plural; molim vas adds politeness.

exercises.prompt: Ask someone politely to say it once more.
exercises.feedback: Recite is the polite or plural imperative of reći.

exercises.prompt: Add a polite closing to Čekajte ovde.
exercises.feedback: Molim vas is a useful polite addition to a request.

lessons.unit_objective: Make requests and connect ideas.

lessons.title: Compare things
lessons.objective: Use common comparative adjectives and a simple comparison.
lessons.teaching_note: Common comparative forms include veći, manji and bolji. Use od with a noun phrase (veći od Beograda) and nego što with a clause (veći nego što sam mislio). Comparative forms may be irregular, so learn high-frequency pairs as vocabulary.

examples.target: Ovaj grad je manji od Beograda.
examples.english: This city is smaller than Belgrade.

exercises.prompt: What is a common comparative form of dobar ("good")?
exercises.feedback: Bolji means better and is an irregular comparative of dobar.

exercises.feedback: Veći is the comparative form meaning bigger.

exercises.prompt: Complete the comparison: Ovaj hotel je veći ___ što sam mislio.
exercises.feedback: Nego što introduces the clause in this comparison: bigger than I thought.

prompt_segments.text: Ovaj hotel je veći ___ što sam mislio.

lessons.title: Say how often
lessons.objective: Use common frequency adverbs and place them naturally in a sentence.
lessons.teaching_note: Često means often, ponekad means sometimes, and nikad means never. Adverbs can move for emphasis, but a simple position before the verb is a useful starting point. Nikad is usually paired with ne before the verb: Nikad ne kasnim, “I am never late.”

exercises.prompt: Which word means “sometimes”?
exercises.feedback: Ponekad means sometimes; često means often and nikad means never.

exercises.prompt: Translate: I often drink tea.
exercises.feedback: Često means often, and pijem is “I drink.”

exercises.prompt: Make the statement say "I am never late": Nikad ___ kasnim.
exercises.feedback: In this common negative pattern, nikad is followed by ne and the verb.

lessons.title: Notice completed and ongoing actions
lessons.objective: Recognize a few imperfective and perfective verb pairs.
lessons.teaching_note: Many verbs occur in aspectual pairs. Pisati often presents writing as an activity; napisati presents writing as completed. Kupovati and kupiti can contrast repeated or ongoing buying with a completed purchase. Aspect is not simply past versus present; learn each verb with example sentences.

examples.note: The participle agrees with the speaker.

exercises.prompt: Which verb commonly presents the action of writing as completed?
exercises.feedback: Napisati commonly presents writing as completed; aspect depends on context.

exercises.prompt: Translate: I am writing a message.
exercises.feedback: Pišem is the present form of pisati, commonly used for an ongoing activity.

exercises.prompt: Give the common perfective partner of kupovati.
exercises.feedback: Kupiti is a common perfective partner of kupovati.

lessons.title: Connect ideas with because and if
lessons.objective: Join short clauses with common conjunctions.
lessons.teaching_note: I means and, ali means but, jer means because, and ako means if. Kad or kada can mean when. Serbian and Montenegrin often use da + present in subordinate clauses where English uses an infinitive, as in Želim da idem, “I want to go.”

examples.target: Želim da idem, ali nemam vremena.
examples.english: I want to go, but I don't have time.

examples.target: Ostajem kod kuće jer pada kiša.
examples.english: I am staying home because it is raining.

exercises.prompt: Which word means “because”?
exercises.feedback: Jer introduces a reason and means because.

exercises.prompt: Join the ideas with ali: Želim da idem. Nemam vremena.
accepted_answers: Želim da idem, ali nemam vremena
Želim da idem, ali nemam vremena.
exercises.feedback: Ali means but and links the contrasting ideas.

exercises.prompt: Translate: If you have time, come. Use informal singular.
exercises.feedback: Ako means if; imaš and dođi address one person informally.

lessons.title: Add detail with koji
lessons.objective: Use a simple relative clause to identify a person or thing.
lessons.teaching_note: Koji, koja and koje introduce relative clauses and agree with the noun they describe. The form also changes for grammatical case, so treat these first sentences as patterns, not a complete paradigm. A relative clause adds information about a noun.

examples.target: To je čovek koji živi ovde.
alternatives: To je čovjek koji živi ovdje.
examples.english: That is the man who lives here.
That is the woman I know.
This is a place that I like.

exercises.prompt: Choose a common form to describe žena: To je žena ___ poznajem.
exercises.feedback: Koju is the feminine accusative form needed for the object of poznajem.

accepted_answers: To je čovek koji živi ovde

To je čovjek koji živi ovdje.

exercises.prompt: What information does a relative clause add?
accepted_answers: It adds information about a noun.
exercises.feedback: A relative clause identifies or describes a noun, as koji živi ovde describes a man.

lessons.title: Soften a request
lessons.objective: Use a polite conditional question and a simple if-clause.
lessons.teaching_note: A conditional can soften a request. Da li biste mogli da ponovite? means “Could you repeat that?” Biste is the polite conditional form of biti. Ako imam vremena, doći ću means “If I have time, I will come”; the future form appears in the main clause.

examples.target: Da li biste mogli da ponovite?

examples.english: If I have time, I will come.

examples.target: Da li biste mogli da govorite sporije?

exercises.prompt: Which is a polite way to ask someone to repeat?

options.text: Da li biste mogli da ponovite?

exercises.feedback: Biste mogli is a polite conditional request.

exercises.prompt: Complete the polite request: Da li biste mogli da ___ sporije?
exercises.feedback: Govorite is the polite or plural form used in this request.

prompt_segments.text: Da li biste mogli da ___ sporije?

exercises.prompt: Complete: Ako imam vremena, ___ ću. (I will come.)
exercises.feedback: Doći ću is a future form meaning I will come.

lessons.unit_objective: Use what you know in practical conversations.

lessons.title: Review: ask for help while traveling
lessons.objective: Combine greetings, directions, polite requests and useful variants.
lessons.teaching_note: Use the phrases together rather than as isolated translations. A traveler can greet someone, ask where a station is, request slower speech and thank the helper. Gde/gdje and levo/lijevo are useful Ekavian/Ijekavian pairs; both are understood widely.

examples.english: Good day. Where is the station?

exercises.prompt: You need the station. Which question is useful?
exercises.feedback: Gde je stanica? asks where the station is; Gdje is also accepted.

exercises.prompt: Politely ask a person to speak more slowly.
exercises.feedback: Možete li da... is a polite question pattern.

exercises.prompt: Thank the person for their help.
exercises.feedback: Hvala vam na pomoći means thank you for your help.

lessons.unit_objective: Use what you know in practical conversations.

lessons.title: Capstone: plan a weekend
lessons.objective: Use a short conversation to make plans, compare options and agree on a time.
lessons.teaching_note: Combine future plans, time expressions, places, comparisons and questions. Keep the conversation simple: suggest a place, ask when the other person is free, make a plan, and confirm it. Reuse the forms you know; variants such as sjutra/sutra remain acceptable.

examples.note: The adjective agrees with the person addressed.

examples.english: We can go to the city.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks if a woman is free tomorrow?
exercises.feedback: Slobodna agrees with a woman; slobodan is the masculine form. Sutra means tomorrow.

exercises.prompt: Suggest: “We can go to the city.”
exercises.feedback: Možemo means we can; u grad expresses movement into the city.

exercises.prompt: Confirm the plan and say "See you tomorrow," using either common form.
exercises.feedback: Both sutra and sjutra are used. The phrase vidimo se is a common reciprocal farewell.

lessons.unit_objective: Use what you know in practical conversations.

lessons.title: Check in
lessons.objective: Ask for a room and a key.
lessons.teaching_note: Imate li…? is a polite way to ask whether someone has something. Jednu sobu is the form used when requesting one room.

examples.target: Dobar dan. Imate li slobodnu sobu?
examples.english: Good day. Do you have a room available?

exercises.prompt: How can you ask for a room?
exercises.feedback: Jednu sobu, molim asks for one room.

exercises.prompt: Write “One room, please.”
exercises.feedback: Jednu sobu, molim asks for one room.

exercises.prompt: Evo ključa.
exercises.feedback: Evo ključa means “Here is the key.”

lessons.unit_objective: Handle a stay, shopping and asking for help.

lessons.title: At the shop
lessons.objective: Ask the price and pay by card.
lessons.teaching_note: Koliko košta? asks the price. Mogu li…? is a polite way to ask if you can do something.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks to pay by card?
exercises.feedback: Koliko košta? asks how much something costs.

exercises.prompt: Write “How much does it cost?”
exercises.feedback: Koliko košta? asks how much something costs.

exercises.prompt: Pet eura.
exercises.feedback: Pet eura means “five euros.”

lessons.unit_objective: Handle a stay, shopping and asking for help.

lessons.title: Find a pharmacy
lessons.objective: Ask where a pharmacy is and understand a direction.
lessons.teaching_note: Gdje je…? asks where something is; Serbian Ekavian also uses Gde je…? Desno means right.

examples.english: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy?
The pharmacy is nearby, on the right.

exercises.prompt: Which word means “right” as a direction?
exercises.feedback: Gdje je apoteka? asks where the pharmacy is. Gde is the Ekavian form.

exercises.prompt: Write “Where is the pharmacy?”
exercises.feedback: Gdje je apoteka? asks where the pharmacy is. Gde is the Ekavian form.

exercises.prompt: Apoteka je blizu.
exercises.feedback: Apoteka je blizu means “The pharmacy is nearby.”

lessons.unit_objective: Handle a stay, shopping and asking for help.

lessons.title: Ask for help
lessons.objective: Say you need help or a doctor.
lessons.teaching_note: Treba mi… means “I need…”. Izvinite can politely get someone’s attention.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means “I need a doctor”?
exercises.feedback: Treba mi pomoć means “I need help.”

exercises.prompt: Write “I need help.”
exercises.feedback: Treba mi pomoć means “I need help.”

exercises.prompt: Treba mi doktor.
exercises.feedback: Treba mi doktor means “I need a doctor.”

lessons.unit_objective: Handle a stay, shopping and asking for help.

lessons.title: A day out
lessons.objective: Combine a question, direction and polite thanks.
lessons.teaching_note: Use Gdje je…? to ask for a place, and Hvala to thank the person who helps you.

examples.english: Excuse me, where is the bus station?

exercises.prompt: Which answer means “straight ahead, then right”?
exercises.feedback: Hvala and Hvala vam both express thanks.

exercises.prompt: Write “Thank you.”
exercises.feedback: Hvala and Hvala vam both express thanks.

exercises.prompt: Jednu kartu, molim.
exercises.feedback: Jednu kartu, molim means “One ticket, please.”
